claims.text: In equiatomic Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti, superconducting behavior is governed by the degree of chemical short-range order developed during annealing.
Chemical short-range order alters local electron scattering and pairing interactions.
The as-cast equiatomic Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti alloy has a random elemental distribution.
Annealing at 700 K for 10–40 hours promotes chemical short-range order.
The proposed 700 K annealing treatments can develop short-range order without causing complete phase segregation.
High-vacuum annealing prevents oxidation and unwanted phase formation.
Systematically varying annealing time tunes the degree of chemical short-range order.
X-ray pair-distribution-function analysis can quantify the degree of chemical short-range order relative to the as-cast state.
Enhanced chemical short-range order modifies local electronic environments.
Enhanced chemical short-range order changes electron-scattering rates.
Enhanced chemical short-range order changes the uniformity of the superconducting gap.
Short-range-order-induced local environments can enhance or suppress Tc depending on whether they optimize or disrupt electron pairing.
Samples with greater chemical short-range order will exhibit a systematic Tc difference relative to the as-cast baseline.
The extent of chemical short-range order increases with longer annealing time.
The as-cast baseline has minimal chemical short-range order.
The proposed superconducting effect applies only when annealing produces short-range order without macroscopic phase segregation or secondary-phase formation.
Extreme chemical ordering or phase segregation lies outside the hypothesis's boundary conditions.
